description:
🌙 BZLUNAR — Two Brothers. One Universe. Three Minds.

We’re Badr, Zain, and Khaled, a team passionate about space exploration and engineering. Our project, Lunar Landing Site Navigator, helps users compare lunar landing sites using Sun and Earth positions.

🚀 We welcome anyone interested in coding, astronomy, lunar science, data analysis, design, and research. Beginners are welcome!

Let’s explore the Moon together! 🌕
summary:
Project BZLUNAR is an interactive lunar mission-planning platform designed to help researchers, engineers, and future mission planners identify and evaluate potential lunar landing sites. By transforming NASA lunar imagery, elevation data, and astronomical calculations into an immersive 3D environment, BZLUNAR makes complex lunar surface conditions easier to explore and understand.

The platform features 26 carefully selected lunar locations, including the lunar south pole, Shackleton Crater, Mons Malapert, sunlit highlands, historic Apollo landing sites, and regions of the far side. Users can explore the Moon in realistic 3D, select dates between 2025 and 2030, and compare how changing solar illumination and Earth visibility affect individual landing locations. By visualizing the Sun and Earth relative to the actual terrain horizon, the platform helps assess potential illumination periods, communication opportunities, and lander power availability.

As humanity prepares for a sustained return to the Moon, choosing the right landing site and timing is critical. BZLUNAR aims to make lunar exploration data more accessible, understandable, and useful for informed mission planning.
details:
Project BZLUNAR: Lunar Landing Site Navigator Details:

1. What does our project do, and how does it work?

We built BZLUNAR because we wanted to make exploring and understanding the Moon more interactive and meaningful. Our project is a 3D lunar exploration and landing-site analysis platform that allows users to explore different parts of the Moon and investigate whether they could be suitable for future missions.

The platform includes 26 selected lunar locations, ranging from the lunar south pole and Shackleton Crater to Mons Malapert, historic Apollo landing sites, and areas on the far side of the Moon.

Users can explore the Moon through an interactive 3D environment, zoom into specific locations, and select different dates between 2025 and 2030. They can then examine how sunlight reaches each location and how the surrounding terrain affects visibility of Earth. This helps users understand two important challenges for lunar missions: keeping landers powered through solar energy and maintaining communication with Earth.

2. What benefits does it offer?

One thing we realized while working on this challenge is that choosing a landing site involves much more than finding an interesting location on the Moon. Sunlight, terrain, and communication all play important roles.

We wanted to bring these factors together instead of making users search through multiple maps and datasets. BZLUNAR provides one place where they can explore locations, compare different dates, and better understand the conditions that future lunar missions may face.

It can also be useful for students, educators, researchers, and anyone interested in understanding how space missions are planned.

3. What impact do we hope to make?

Our goal is to make lunar science easier to explore and understand. As humanity moves toward returning to the Moon and establishing a longer-term presence there, understanding the lunar environment will become increasingly important.

We hope BZLUNAR can help people look at the Moon differently. Instead of seeing it as just a distant object in the sky, users can explore its actual terrain, investigate different regions, and understand some of the decisions that go into planning a mission.

We also hope the project encourages more students to become interested in space science, engineering, and exploration.

4. What tools and technologies did we use?

Building BZLUNAR required combining several technologies and scientific data sources. Our work involved:

  • WebGL and 3D graphics: For creating the interactive 3D lunar environment.
  • NASA lunar imagery: To represent the Moon using real scientific imagery.
  • NASA LOLA data: To work with lunar elevation and terrain information.
  • NASA/JPL ephemeris data: To support calculations related to the positions of the Sun and Earth.
  • WebGL shaders and terrain rendering: To create the visual environment and represent lunar surface features.
  • Mission control interface and UX design: To make the platform easier to navigate and understand.

Each part of the project contributed to turning scientific information into something people can actually interact with.

5. What makes our project creative?

What makes BZLUNAR different is how we brought everything together. We did not want to create another static lunar map or a website that simply displays information. We wanted users to feel like they were exploring the Moon themselves.

Being able to move around a 3D Moon, select a landing location, change the date, and investigate how sunlight and Earth visibility change makes the experience much more engaging.

We also wanted to make scientific information less intimidating. Someone with no background in astrophysics should still be able to open the platform, explore a location, and begin understanding the challenges behind landing on the Moon.

6. What factors did our team consider?

Throughout development, we constantly asked ourselves what a future lunar mission would actually need to consider.

Some of the most important factors were:

  • Terrain: What does the surrounding landscape look like, and how does elevation affect the environment?
  • Sunlight: When does a location receive sunlight, and for how long?
  • Communication: When can a lander potentially maintain visibility of Earth?
  • Timing: How do these conditions change depending on the selected date?
  • Location selection: Which lunar regions would be interesting and valuable to investigate?
  • Usability: How can we make a technically complex platform simple enough for anyone to explore?

Ultimately, BZLUNAR started with a simple idea: we wanted to make exploring the Moon more than just looking at pictures of it. We wanted people to interact with real lunar information, ask questions, compare locations, and understand the challenges that stand between us and humanity's next steps on the Moon.
